entry.evidence: The genesis of Paleoproterozoic high-grade martite-microplaty ore (in short hematite ore) deposits in the Hamersley Province (Fig. 1) remains a matter of debate.

sequences.source_document: Angerer et al. 2022, Ore Geology Reviews 144, 104840 (published PDF)

steps.action: States the aim: to understand the debated transformation of BIF to hematite ore through the textures and chemistry of iron oxides from alteration zones.
steps.quote: The present contribution aims to better understand the highly debated transformation

steps.action: Takes the rival genetic models from the literature: multistage hydrothermal models, the supergene-metamorphic goethite-dehydration model, and non-classical crystallisation by coalescence of colloidal hematite.
steps.quote: The main competing concept is the supergene-metamorphic model (Morris, 1985; Morris and Fletcher, 1987)

steps.action: Adds a methodological question: iron oxide trace-element behaviour in low-temperature hydrothermal systems is poorly known and needs more data.
steps.quote: To develop robust models for trace metal dependencies, we need more data from metal-depleted low-temperature hydrothermal systems.

steps.action: Samples drill cores intersecting the ore-controlling faults (Southern Batter, SE Prong, Central, East Footwall and Whaleback Fault splays), satellite deposits, and distal least-altered BIF.
steps.quote: Several diamond drillholes from Mt. Tom Price that intersect the Southern Batter Fault have been sampled

steps.action: Describes hand-specimen and microscopic petrography of least-altered BIF, the distal and intermediate hydrothermal alteration zones, proximal hematite-altered BIF, and ore.
steps.quote: Drill core EC0661D at Eastern Ridge reveals a rare occurrence of fresh BIF.

steps.action: Builds a descriptive paragenetic sequence of oxide generations (stages 0, 1a, 1b, 2) from textures, supported by EPMA element maps showing zoned, epitaxial microplaty hematite growth.
steps.quote: Based on our observations, a descriptive paragenetic sequence for oxides involved in the BIF to high-grade hematite ore transformation is established

steps.action: Measures trace elements in magnetite, martite, mosaic and microplaty hematite by LA-ICPMS in three laboratories and summarises the abundances by oxide type.
steps.quote: Element concentrations in oxides are highly variable across the samples set and can span over three orders of magnitude

steps.action: Defines a Dales Gorge BIF reference magnetite for normalisation, excludes Si and Ca because of inclusions, and fixes a quartile-overlap criterion for similarity.
steps.quote: a similarity between two samples is considered robust when both medians lie within the others’ 1. and 3. quartile range.

steps.action: Derives expected relative compatibilities of cations in magnetite and hematite from charge and coupled substitution, because no low-temperature partition coefficients exist.
steps.quote: we approach this problem with a consideration of the theoretical differences in cation compatibility based on cation charge

steps.action: Compares normalised signatures across the Mt. Tom Price alteration zones and ore; finds a conservative Ga-Cr-Ti-Co-Cu-Ni suite linking stage 1a, stage 1b and stage 2 by inheritance.
steps.quote: this strongly advocates for an alteration sequence consisting of stage 1 BIF alteration

steps.action: Plots microplaty hematite element abundances against distance to the Central and Whaleback Faults and identifies depletion, enrichment and conservative trends that differ between the two faults.
steps.quote: Approaching the Central Fault, elements systematically fractionate following three distinct trends

steps.action: Proposes a cryptic pre-ore alteration stage 1CF/WF at Mt. Whaleback, recorded only in hematite chemistry distal to the faults.
steps.quote: a chemical modification of iron oxides prior to fault-controlled hematite mineralisation is suggested.

steps.action: Computes dissolved cation speciation and Eh-pH predominance for an assumed meteoric stage 2 fluid with The Geochemist's Workbench, to explain the fault-proximal depletion and the Al pH effect.
steps.quote: according to fluid speciation calculation using The Geochemist’s Workbench

steps.action: Compares Eastern Ridge altered-BIF magnetite and eastern satellite ore hematite with Mt. Tom Price signatures; infers a cryptic proto-ore stage 1EP and that the eastern ores are related to one another.
steps.quote: Ore-forming hematite in the eastern province samples are thus chemically related to each other.

steps.action: Uses element ratios and sums as proxies (Al/Mg for maturity, Ni/Pb and Cr/U for source rock, Cu+Ni+Pb+Zn for salinity or temperature, the Nadoll Ti+V vs Al+Mn diagram for temperature) to rank the ore zones.
steps.quote: Thus, the Al/Mg ratio (Fig. 14a) is a measure of relative maturity of stage-2 hematite mineralisation

steps.action: Reanalyses the same hematite dataset with principal component analysis; it discriminates the orebodies and fault proximity and groups Whaleback Fault ore with SE Prong and the eastern ores.
steps.quote: The multivariate data analyses of hematite composition successfully discriminate orebodies and fault-proximity within orebodies based on element correlation.

steps.action: Rules out dynamic recrystallisation, and solid-state diffusion at the relevant temperatures, as the mechanism of hydrothermal magnetite re-equilibration.
steps.quote: This mechanism can be ruled out here, as syn-metamorphic BIF deformation preceded ore formation.

steps.action: Tentatively keeps coupled dissolution-reprecipitation (CDR) as the most likely magnetite re-equilibration mechanism, citing porosity and literature analogues.
steps.quote: we tentatively consider CDR as the most likely scenario for the modification of magnetite textures and chemistries

steps.action: Proposes coupled oxidative dissolution-transfer-reprecipitation (CDTR) as the microplaty hematite-forming mechanism, consistent with inheritance and the fault-proximity gradients.
steps.quote: Microplaty hematite mineralisation may here be described as a coupled oxidative dissolution-transfer-reprecipitation process (CDTR)

steps.action: Sets the oxide chemistry against published fluid inclusion, stable isotope, geochronology and structural data to build fluid-rock models for each fault-controlled ore system.
steps.quote: based on evidence derived from rock alteration, oxide textures, mineral chemistry, and published information

steps.action: Proposes a new two-stage structurally controlled fluid-flow model for Mt. Whaleback: cryptic stage 1CF/1WF proto-ore followed by stage 2 meteoric or reservoir-controlled mineralisation.
steps.quote: Based on hematite chemistry in ore, a novel fluid-flow/alteration model is proposed

steps.action: Explains the conflicting observation that ore at the Whaleback Fault is juxtaposed against fresh country rock by post-mineralisation fault reactivation, keeping the structural-control model.
steps.quote: This can be explained with post-mineralisation reactivation, which is supported by abundant ore clasts within the fault

steps.action: Argues that hematite nucleation and zoning, inheritance of alteration signatures, depletion towards the Central Fault, and U/Pb ages are incompatible with goethite dehydration, particle coalescence and post-ore alteration.
steps.quote: This is not expected for hematite growth via goethite dehydration or by particle coalescence.

steps.action: Concludes that the oxide chemistry supports multistage hydrothermal models at Mt. Tom Price and a new two-stage structurally controlled hydrothermal model at Mt. Whaleback.
steps.quote: a new two-stage, structurally controlled hydrothermal model is offered for Mt. Whaleback, despite the apparent obliteration of all proto-ore.

No: genesis known only from mineral and chemical traces
Explain the ore genesis by fingerprinting fluid-rock interaction in iron oxides
Yes: multistage hydrothermal vs supergene-metamorphic vs particle coalescence (and post-ore alteration)
Partly: qualitative expectations (growth zoning, gradient direction towards faults, inheritance)
Found: drill cores across natural fault-controlled alteration zones

tree.answer: Yes: several faults, two major deposits and satellite orebodies
Partly: PCA on the same data agrees; published isotope and fluid-inclusion data are compatible
Multistage hydrothermal genesis kept as best explanation; rivals argued incompatible

end.claim: In-situ iron oxide chemistry supports post-metamorphic, structurally controlled, multistage hydrothermal hematite ore formation at Mt. Tom Price and Mt. Whaleback, including a new two-stage model with cryptic proto-ore alteration at Mt. Whaleback.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing normalised oxide signatures across alteration zones and ore, which showed conservative, inherited element suites, is what links ore hematite to the earlier hydrothermal alteration; without it, neither the multistage model nor the cryptic stage 1 would exist.

gates.evidence: Sampling targeted drill cores intersecting the faults that the hydrothermal structural-control model holds responsible (p. 5), so a hypothesis partly directed acquisition. The claim could have failed, for example if gradients had shown enrichment towards the Central Fault as a goethite origin implies (p. 27), but the expectations were qualitative and set after the data. The similarity criterion (p. 15) and the Nadoll diagram fields were applied, with no statement that anything was fixed before the data were seen.

limits: The supplied XML text holds only captions, so body steps are located by printed page. No peer-review file was supplied, although the acknowledgements mention pre-submission and two anonymous reviews; no review sequence could be coded. Sub-claims and their statuses: CDR as the magnetite re-equilibration mechanism is tentative (best_explanation, p. 24). CDTR as the main mineralisation process is proposed, best_explanation (p. 27). The ratio proxies for maturity, source and salinity/temperature are qualitative rankings without uncertainty, not an estimate_with_resolution (pp. 21-22). Hematite mineralisation temperatures possibly above 110 °C are left open (p. 27). The authors state that no partition coefficients are available (p. 16), that Mt. Tom Price lacks data on structural control of stage 2 chemistry (p. 26), and that the influence of precursor phases remains speculative (p. 19). Mosaic hematite is excluded from detailed interpretation. About 40 samples were analysed; the selection criteria for the microanalysed subset are not given. Inference: the order of fieldwork, analysis and model building cannot be reconstructed from the text, and the rival exclusions are argued qualitatively rather than by a pre-specified crucial test.

disagreements.support: Epitaxial nucleation, zoned growth of microplaty hematite, and depletion of trace elements towards the Central Fault are argued to be incompatible with hematite inheriting its chemistry from goethite.
disagreements.quote: Several key observations challenge different genetic models, particularly the supergene-metamorphic model (Morris, 1985; Morris and Fletcher, 1987)

disagreements.target: Non-classical crystallisation by particle coalescence (Egglseder et al., 2019)
disagreements.support: Nucleation on martite or globular hematite surfaces and protracted zoned growth indicate precipitation from a hydrothermal solution.
disagreements.quote: This is not expected for hematite growth via goethite dehydration or by particle coalescence.

disagreements.support: Chemical signatures of the hydrothermal carbonate-silicate-oxide alteration zones are inherited in ore and in hematite-altered BIF close to ore.
disagreements.quote: is not compatible with post-ore alteration as suggested by Morris and Kneeshaw (2011).

disagreements.target: Whaleback Fault as a post-ore structure (Morris and Kneeshaw, 2011; Powell et al., 1999; Ronaszeki 1992, 2010; Thorne et al., [...]
disagreements.support: Fault-proximity trace-element trends in hematite, lower δ18O in the fault (Angerer et al., 2013a), and ore clasts in the fault point to structural control followed by reactivation.
disagreements.quote: Structurally controlled oxide formation and/or re-equilibration related to Whaleback Fault is supported by oxygen isotope data

disagreements.target: Hematite mineralisation temperatures of 60-110 °C (Morris, 1985; Thorne et al., 2009)
disagreements.support: Ti+V vs Al+Mn compositions plot in the 200-300 °C empirical field of Nadoll et al. (2014), although the authors note this may reflect inheritance.
disagreements.quote: Temperatures of hematite mineralisation, previously implied to be ranging between 60 and 110 ◦C (Morris, 1985; Thorne et al., 2009), may also be higher

disagreements.target: Morris and Kneeshaw (2011) dismissal of protracted hydrothermal growth from phosphate U/Pb ages
disagreements.support: Published U/Pb ages (Rasmussen et al., 2007b) fit regional extensional phases and multiple hydrothermal pulses; the paper offers no new data on this point.
disagreements.quote: Morris and Kneeshaw (2011) dismissed this argument
